result: Middle-aged adults recruited for the study had clinically normal hearing thresholds (≤25 dB HL for 250 Hz-8 kHz), normal otoscopy, comparable outer hair cell function up to 4 kHz, no severe tinnitus or hyperacusis, comparable noise exposure and working memory scores, but showed threshold differences at extended high frequencies (>8 kHz) and some subclinical outer hair cell dysfunction above 4 kHz.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accepted the participant characterization, with one reviewer stating 'The study begins with a comprehensive assessment of the hearing status of the human listeners. The only differences found between the young adult (YA) and middle aged (MA) groups are in thresholds at frequencies > 10 kHz and DPOAE amplitudes at frequencies > 5 kHz.' No concerns were raised about these baseline measurements.

result: In humans, EFRs to 1024 Hz amplitude modulation showed statistically significant age-related decreases in middle-aged adults compared to young adults, with decreases selective only for the 1024 Hz modulation frequency (putative auditory nerve generators) but not for slower AM rates with putative generators in midbrain or cortex.
evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the finding, one reviewer questioned why significant differences were found only at 1024 Hz, noting 'previous studies employing SAM or RAM tones very similar to the ones employed here were able to show age effects already at lower modulation freqs. of ~100Hz' and asked whether the authors tried extracting EFR strength by summing multiple harmonics. This suggests the selectivity finding may be methodologically dependent rather than definitively established.

result: Middle-aged gerbils showed no loss of hearing thresholds but exhibited a selective decrease in EFR amplitudes for AM rates at 1024 Hz, similar to middle-aged humans.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the cross-species EFR findings without challenge. One reviewer stated the study 'showing that amplitudes decrease more rapidly with increasing envelope frequency for MA than for YA in both species,' and another noted 'the results show clearly a decrease of neural phase-locking to high modulation frequencies in both middle-aged humans and gerbils.'

result: Histological analysis in gerbils showed significant decreases in afferent synapse counts (up to 20% losses) in middle-aged gerbils, and EFR amplitudes at 1024 Hz were significantly correlated with the number of remaining cochlear synapses, confirming EFRs as a sensitive metric of CND.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this finding. One stated 'The histological analysis of the gerbil cochleae shows that there were, on average, 20% fewer IHC-AN synapses at the 3 kHz place in MA relative to YA, and the number of synapses per IHC was correlated with the EFR amplitude at 1024 Hz.' Another reviewer noted this provides 'strong support to the view that normal aging in humans leads to auditory nerve synaptic loss.'

result: Behavioral assessments using QuickSIN revealed age-related speech-in-noise deficits under challenging conditions, with behavioral deficits emerging only at the most challenging SNR levels (0 dB), while performance was matched between age groups at moderate SNRs.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these behavioral findings without challenge. One reviewer stated 'The correct understanding of keywords decreased more rapidly with decreasing SNR in MA than in YA, with a noticeable difference at 0 dB,' and another noted the study showed 'reduced speech-in-noise intelligibility evidenced in middle-aged individuals.'

result: Pupil-indexed listening effort increased with age even when behavioral performance was matched, with middle-aged adults showing consistently higher pupillary responses during QuickSIN performance at SNR levels prior to when overt behavioral deficits were observed, and perceptual deficits in listening effort appearing prior to behavioral changes.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed the listening effort findings. One stated 'pupillary slope (a proxy for listening effort) increased more rapidly with decreasing SNR for MA than for YA, with the largest differences at SNRs between 5 and 15 dB.' Another noted 'pupillometry measurements conducted during the QuickSIN task suggest increased listening efforts in middle-aged participants.'

result: Pupil-indexed listening effort at a moderate SNR (10 dB) was a better predictor of behavioral performance at a more challenging SNR (0 dB) than concurrent measures, suggesting that the amount of effort required to maintain ceiling performance at moderate SNRs is predictive of behavioral performance at harder task difficulties.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this predictive relationship. One reviewer noted the authors 'report that a linear combination of audiometric threshold, EFR amplitude at 1024 Hz, and a few measures of pupillary slope is predictive of speech perception at 0 dB SNR,' implicitly accepting the predictive value of pupillary measures.

result: An elastic net regression model suggested that CND (measured by EFRs), listening effort (pupillometry), and subclinical changes in hearing thresholds all provided complementary contributions to explaining variance on QuickSIN performance at 0 dB SNR.
evaluation: One reviewer raised a methodological concern: 'Unless I misunderstood, the predictive power of the final model was not tested on held out data. The standard way to fit and test such model would be to split the data into two segments, one for training and hyperparameter optimization, and one for testing.' While the authors later clarified the modeling approach, this indicates uncertainty about the generalizability of the model's predictive power.

result: CND was associated with decreased neural coding fidelity, increased listening effort, and contributed to speech perception difficulties in middle-aged adults with normal audiometric thresholds.
evaluation: Reviewers provided strong support for this main conclusion. The editor stated the findings 'pose compelling evidence that cochlear synaptopathy is associated with a significant part of hearing difficulties in complex environments,' and another reviewer noted the paper 'shows that these difficulties can be reasonably well accounted for by this sensory disorder (CND), but also that listening effort, i.e. a top-down factor, further contributes to this problem.'

result: CND may ultimately lead to listening fatigue and social withdrawal, as middle-aged adults expend more effort to maintain behavioral performance.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this speculative consequence without challenge. The claims are presented as reasonable inferences from the data on increased listening effort, and no reviewer questioned this interpretation.

result: Subtle changes in hearing thresholds within the clinically normal range affected speech-in-noise performance, lending support to the idea that the definition of clinically 'normal' hearing may need revision.
evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accepted this finding. One noted 'Even though both young and middle-aged adults had clinically normal-hearing thresholds, subtle changes within this normal range affected speech-in-noise performance,' and the broader acceptance of the study's findings about hidden hearing loss supports this claim.
